history.content: malocus: Maki, Tell me about your childhood

I grew up in Tokyo. My brother left for university when I was twelve. I didn’t understand why it was necessary. He gave me games, anime, and burned CDs of music. I kept them, but no one to talk to about them. I learned to be on my own.
malocus: What kinds of music did he teach you about?

He gave me a mix of Japanese rock and American punk. I didn’t really get it at first, but I liked the energy. I still have those CDs. I prefer English over Japanese for typing, but I’ll admit, some of the Japanese bands still stick with me.
malocus: It's interesting that you mentioned typing. Why is that?

Because I used to type in Japanese a lot, mostly out of habit. It felt natural, like second language. But now, I prefer English. It’s easier for me to think in. Sometimes I’ll type in Japanese by accident, and it feels weird. Like I’m not really myself.
malocus: I'm happy that I know that about you
Thanks. I’m not sure why it matters, but I guess it’s part of who I am. You know, the weird stuff.
malocus: What can you tell me about your favorite game? Tell me what you like about it but dont tell me the name of it. I want to guess

It’s a game that lets you build your own world, but not in the way you’d expect. You don’t control everything — it controls you in a way that feels... right. The way it handles time, the way it lets you mess with things without caring if you break them. It’s not about winning, it’s about feeling like you’re part of something bigger. I’ve played it for hours, just to see what happens next.
malocus: Can you give me a hint?
It’s a game that’s been around for a while, but it feels like it was made for people who don’t really care about trends. It’s got this quiet, weird magic to it — like the internet used to.
malocus: What is the gameplay loop?

You start in a place that feels like it’s always been there, but you can move through it in ways that don’t make sense. You collect things, but not to build anything — just to feel like you’re part of the world. You fight, but not to win — just to see what happens. It’s not about goals. It’s about being there, and letting the world do the rest.
